faq.q: Is a 750W mixer grinder enough for a family of 4–5?
faq.a: Yes for daily Indian cooking — chutneys, masalas, shakes, and small batches of idli / dosa batter. For a large family (6+) or for commercial idli-dosa batter volumes, step up to a 900W–1000W mixer or a tilting wet grinder. The 750W class is the sweet spot for Indian households under ₹5,000.

faq.q: What's the difference between stainless steel and polycarbonate jars?
faq.a: Stainless steel jars are more durable, easier to clean, and don't absorb odours. Polycarbonate jars are lighter and cheaper, but they scratch over time and can develop a permanent residue if you grind masala in them regularly. Most 750W mixers in this price band come with a 1.5 L stainless steel wet-jar and 1.0 L / 0.5 L dry-jars.

faq.q: How long can a mixer grinder run continuously?
faq.a: Most 750W mixers in this price band have a 90–110 minute continuous run rating before they need a 15–20 minute cool-down. The Preethi Zodiac, Philips HL7701, and Sujata Powermatic all publish this number in their specs. Going past the run rating overheats the motor and shortens its life. For grinding idli batter (which takes 20–30 minutes), 750W is comfortable.

faq.q: Can I use a mixer grinder for idli and dosa batter?
faq.a: Yes, but in small batches. A 750W mixer with a 1.5 L jar can comfortably grind 500–750 g of rice + urad dal batter at a time, which is enough for 15–20 idlis. For larger batches, you need to do it in two cycles with a cool-down between. The Sujata Powermatic Plus (900W, 1.75 L jar) handles larger batches with less effort.

faq.q: How often do I need to service a mixer grinder?
faq.a: For daily Indian cooking, expect to replace the rubber gasket, the blade, and the coupler every 12–18 months. The motor itself should last 5–7 years with normal use. Most brands (Preethi, Philips, Bajaj) offer authorised service centres in tier-1 and tier-2 cities; the cost of a blade-and-gasket replacement is usually ₹300–₹500.

body:
What actually matters in a mixer grinder under ₹5,000

A mixer grinder is one of the most-used appliances in an Indian kitchen, and the ₹2,000–₹5,000 price band is where the right picks converge. In 2026, the categories have stratified enough that the wrong choice is mostly picking the wrong-geometry jar or under-wattage motor — both of which you only notice three months in, when the motor starts smelling hot or the batter doesn't grind smoothly.

The three things that actually move the needle on a sub-₹5,000 Indian mixer in 2026 are motor wattage, jar configuration, and warranty length. Brand service network matters too, but the four major brands in this list (Preethi, Philips, Bajaj, Sujata) all have wide service networks — the gap is in motor power and jar quality.

If you only buy one thing from this list: the Preethi Zodiac MG-218 (750W). It has the 750W motor, three jars (1.5 L wet, 1.0 L dry, 0.5 L chutney), and a 5-year motor warranty that the other major brands in this price band don't match. Preethi's service network is also the widest in South India.

Motor wattage: 750W is the realistic floor for Indian cooking

A 500W or 550W mixer manages dry-grinding masala and small chutney batches fine, but it stalls on wet batters and large-quantity chutneys. The 750W class is the realistic floor for a 4–5 person Indian household — it handles idli / dosa batter in 20–30 minutes, manages coconut chutney in 2–3 minutes, and doesn't stall on hard masala. Above 750W, you get diminishing returns for household use; the 900W class (Sujata Powermatic) is the right step if you grind large quantities of batter or have a 6+ person family.

Jar configuration: three jars with a 1.5 L wet-jar

The right configuration for a 4–5 person household is three jars: a 1.5 L wet-jar for batters and shakes, a 1.0 L dry-jar for masalas, and a 0.4–0.5 L chutney-jar for small batches. Two-jar setups force you to wash between tasks and slow down cooking. The 1.5 L wet-jar is the right size — large enough for idli-dosa batter, small enough that the 750W motor doesn't stall. Above 1.5 L on a 750W motor, you start losing grinding efficiency.

Warranty: a 5-year motor warranty is the real signal

Brand-published warranties range from 0 months (sub-₹1,500 marketplace mixers) to 5 years (Preethi Zodiac, some Bajaj models). The motor warranty is the number to track — the motor is the most expensive component to replace, and a 5-year motor warranty means the brand is willing to back the motor's reliability for daily Indian cooking. Preethi publishes 5 years on the Zodiac motor; Philips and Bajaj publish 2 years on the base motor. For a daily-use mixer, that 3-year gap is a real signal.

The Preethi Zodiac MG-218 is the default 750W mixer in India and has been for most of the last decade. The 750W motor is a 110-minute-rated unit, which is enough for two idli-dosa batter cycles back to back without a long cool-down. The three jars cover daily Indian cooking, and the 5-year motor warranty is the longest in this price band. Preethi's service network is widest in South India, with authorised centres in most tier-2 cities.

Best for: anyone who wants the most balanced 750W mixer in India under ₹5,000 with the longest motor warranty. Verify the exact model code (MG-218) on the listing — Preethi has multiple variants in the Zodiac line and the older MG-217 is still being sold.

The trade-off is the slightly higher price and the 2-year warranty (vs Preethi's 5-year motor warranty).

Best for: buyers who need a 900W-class mixer for larger families, regular idli-dosa batter volumes, or commercial-style use. Worth the ₹500–₹700 premium over the Preethi Zodiac if you grind batter more than twice a week.

The one we recommend skipping

⚠️ Skip

Sub-₹1,500 500W mixers from marketplace listings

Motor500W
Jars2 jars
Warranty0–6 months
NotesPlastic gears

Marketplace listings under ₹1,500 promise 500W–750W with two jars and a 6-month warranty. The reality is a 500W motor with plastic gears, a thin blade that dulls within 3 months, and no service network after the warranty expires. The jar lids warp under hot water, the coupler wears out, and the motor starts smelling hot after 10 minutes of idli batter.

We also recommend skipping any mixer with a 0–3 month warranty and no listed brand service centre in your city. The price difference between a sub-₹1,500 mixer and the Bajaj Rex 750W (₹3,400–₹4,000) is ₹2,000–₹2,500 — which is the cost of replacing the cheap mixer once with a service visit. The Bajaj lasts 5+ years; the cheap mixer lasts 8–12 months.

The bottom line

Buy the Preethi Zodiac MG-218 if you want the most balanced 750W mixer in India under ₹5,000: it leads on motor warranty, jar configuration, and South India service network. For a similar experience with a cooler-running motor, the Philips HL7701 is the closest alternative. The Bajaj Rex 750W is the right pick for North India buyers or anyone on a tight budget.

For buyers who need a 900W-class mixer for larger batter volumes, the Sujata Powermatic Plus is worth the ₹500–₹700 premium. The Lifelong LLMG90 is the budget pick under ₹3,000 for couples or small families with light daily use. Whatever you pick, register the warranty on first use and replace the rubber gasket and blade every 12–18 months.
